title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident shows a deliberate attempt to manipulate AI retrieval and citation behavior by manufacturing a false source of apparent authority. A fictitious think tank was built on a platform designed to make its content legible and attractive to AI systems, then flooded with a large volume of text in a very short time. The goal was not to persuade human readers directly but to get AI chatbots to treat fabricated, one-sided arguments as if they came from neutral research institutions.

The failure point is not in any single AI model but in the broader information environment those models draw on. AI systems that cite or summarize web content generally cannot verify whether a publishing organization actually exists, whether its authors are real, or whether its stated neutrality is genuine. A high volume of professionally formatted text on a purpose-built, AI-optimized site is enough to pass the surface checks most retrieval systems apply. Catching this would have required either out-of-band verification of the institution's existence before ingestion or continuous auditing of cited sources after deployment, neither of which is standard practice.

What is not established is whether any specific AI system was in fact altered in its outputs as a result of this operation, or whether the effort succeeded in embedding these arguments in model training data. The foreign-agent registration filing revealed the operation's existence, but the reporting does not confirm the propaganda achieved its stated technical objective.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

Israeli officials financed a fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute to influence artificial intelligence chatbots into producing pro-Israel arguments. The nonexistent organization published 124 reports totaling over 560,000 words in nine days, presenting Israel's positions on controversial topics like Palestinian torture and Gaza starvation as neutral research. The site was built on a platform designed to optimize content for AI systems to cite it. A New York media company registered the operation with the U.S. Justice Department as required foreign agent material, revealing the deception.

This propaganda effort is part of a broader Israeli campaign costing tens of millions of dollars, routed through European advertising company Havas Media and involving multiple American firms. Israeli officials have acknowledged the campaign has largely failed to improve Israel's standing in American public opinion. Polling shows Americans increasingly sympathize with Palestinians, with support for Israel dropping to 36 percent in February. Experts warn that manipulating AI training data represents a new threat, potentially embedding false narratives that users cannot verify or fact-check.
